A test for three or more groups asks one question: "is there any difference among them?". When the answer is yes, the next question is which groups differ from which. Answering it means running several tests at once, and every extra test is another chance of a false positive. This page shows how to compare groups in pairs while keeping that chance under control. Most "After …" sections pick up an example from [page 8](../catalog/08-three-plus-unmatched.qmd), [page 9](../catalog/09-three-plus-matched.qmd) or [page 13](../survival/13-kaplan-meier.qmd).

::: {.callout-note}
## 💡 How this page works
Run the code blocks in order, from the top: later blocks use the packages and data loaded in the first one.

As on the pages these examples come from, the joint replacement examples use every case, including both cases of patients who had both sides operated on (80 patients in the whole cohort; [page 2](../foundations/02-demographics.qmd#setup) counts them).
:::

## Why many tests mislead {#why-adjust}

A test at the 5% level has a 5% chance of a false positive when there is truly no difference. Run several tests and those chances accumulate. The chance of **at least one** false positive across a set of tests is the **family-wise error rate**. For independent tests at the 5% level it's 1 − 0.95^k^, where k is the number of tests:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
#| warning: false
library(tidyverse)
library(survival)

cohort <- read_csv("data/cohort.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
proms <- read_csv("data/proms_long.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
trial <- read_csv("data/foot_ankle_rct_long.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

tests <- c(1, 3, 6, 10, 20)
false_positives <- tibble(tests, chance_of_a_false_positive = round(1 - 0.95^tests, 2))
false_positives

# four equal groups, six pairwise tests: the chance that at least one gives p < 0.05
1 - ptukey(qnorm(0.975) * sqrt(2), nmeans = 4, df = Inf)
```

## Python

```{python}
import itertools
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pingouin as pg
import scikit_posthocs as sp
from scipy import stats
from statsmodels.stats.multitest import multipletests
from statsmodels.stats.multicomp import pairwise_tukeyhsd
from statsmodels.stats.contingency_tables import mcnemar
from lifelines import CoxPHFitter
from lifelines.statistics import multivariate_logrank_test, pairwise_logrank_test

cohort = pd.read_csv("data/cohort.csv")
proms = pd.read_csv("data/proms_long.csv")
trial = pd.read_csv("data/foot_ankle_rct_long.csv")

tests = np.array([1, 3, 6, 10, 20])
false_positives = pd.DataFrame({"tests": tests, "chance_of_a_false_positive": (1 - 0.95**tests).round(2)})
print(false_positives)

# four equal groups, six pairwise tests: the chance that at least one gives p < 0.05
print(1 - stats.studentized_range.cdf(stats.norm.ppf(0.975) * np.sqrt(2), 4, np.inf))
```
:::

```{python}
#| include: false
chance = false_positives.set_index("tests")["chance_of_a_false_positive"]
chk = {"six": float(chance[6]), "twenty": float(chance[20])}
chk_four = {"four_groups": float(1 - stats.studentized_range.cdf(stats.norm.ppf(0.975) * np.sqrt(2), 4, np.inf))}
```

```{r}
#| include: false
chance <- false_positives$chance_of_a_false_positive
check_agree(list(six = chance[tests == 6], twenty = chance[tests == 20]), reticulate::py$chk)
check_agree(list(four_groups = 1 - ptukey(qnorm(0.975) * sqrt(2), nmeans = 4, df = Inf)), reticulate::py$chk_four)
```

Four groups make six pairs. Six independent tests at the 5% level give a 26% chance of at least one false alarm, even when nothing is going on; twenty tests give 64%. Pairwise comparisons aren't independent, because each group appears in three of the six pairs, so for four groups of equal size the chance is a little lower: about 20% (the last line of the output, 0.203). That's still four times the 5% you meant to allow. Comparing pairs therefore needs an **adjustment**: a stricter rule that keeps the chance of any false positive across the whole set of comparisons at 5%.

::: {.callout-note}
## 💡 In plain language
Buy one lottery ticket and you'll almost certainly lose. Buy twenty and your chance of winning something goes up. Each p-value below 0.05 is a small "win", and with enough tests one will turn up by luck alone. Adjusting the p-values makes each win harder to get, so the overall chance stays where you set it.
:::

## Adjusting p-values: Bonferroni, Holm and Benjamini-Hochberg {#adjusting-p-values}

[Page 8](../catalog/08-three-plus-unmatched.qmd#one-way-anova) found that age differs across the four ASA classes. Here are the six pairwise comparisons, each a Welch t test, with the p-values left as they are (**unadjusted**) and then adjusted three ways:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
age_pairs <- pairwise.t.test(cohort$age, cohort$asa, pool.sd = FALSE,      # Welch t tests
                             p.adjust.method = "none")
unadjusted <- age_pairs$p.value[lower.tri(age_pairs$p.value, diag = TRUE)]  # the six p-values, in pair order

adjusted <- tibble(pair = c("1 vs 2", "1 vs 3", "1 vs 4", "2 vs 3", "2 vs 4", "3 vs 4"),
                   unadjusted,
                   bonferroni = p.adjust(unadjusted, method = "bonferroni"),
                   holm = p.adjust(unadjusted, method = "holm"),
                   bh = p.adjust(unadjusted, method = "BH"))
adjusted |> mutate(across(-pair, \(p) round(p, 4)))
```

## Python

```{python}
asa_pairs = list(itertools.combinations([1, 2, 3, 4], 2))
unadjusted = [stats.ttest_ind(cohort.loc[cohort["asa"] == a, "age"], cohort.loc[cohort["asa"] == b, "age"],
                              equal_var=False).pvalue                    # Welch t tests
              for a, b in asa_pairs]

adjusted = pd.DataFrame({
    "pair": [f"{a} vs {b}" for a, b in asa_pairs],
    "unadjusted": unadjusted,
    "bonferroni": multipletests(unadjusted, method="bonferroni")[1],
    "holm": multipletests(unadjusted, method="holm")[1],
    "bh": multipletests(unadjusted, method="fdr_bh")[1],
})
print(adjusted.round(4))
```
:::

```{python}
#| include: false
chk = {"raw_12": float(unadjusted[0]), "raw_34": float(unadjusted[5]),
       "bonferroni_12": float(adjusted["bonferroni"].iloc[0]), "holm_12": float(adjusted["holm"].iloc[0]),
       "bh_12": float(adjusted["bh"].iloc[0]), "bh_34": float(adjusted["bh"].iloc[5])}
```

```{r}
#| include: false
check_agree(list(raw_12 = adjusted$unadjusted[1], raw_34 = adjusted$unadjusted[6],
                 bonferroni_12 = adjusted$bonferroni[1], holm_12 = adjusted$holm[1],
                 bh_12 = adjusted$bh[1], bh_34 = adjusted$bh[6]),
            reticulate::py$chk)
```

Follow the ASA 1 vs ASA 2 comparison across the row:
- **Unadjusted, p = 0.022:** "significant" on its own, but it's one of six tests.
- **Bonferroni, p = 0.132:** multiplies every p-value by the number of tests (here 6). Simple, but the strictest: it often throws away real differences.
- **Holm, p = 0.044:** a step-down version of Bonferroni. It multiplies the smallest p-value by 6, the next smallest by 5, and so on, but an adjusted p-value can't be smaller than the one before it in that order. ASA 1 vs 2 has the fifth smallest of the six p-values, so it's multiplied by 2: 0.022 × 2 = 0.044. ASA 3 vs 4 has the largest unadjusted p-value (0.030), so it's multiplied by 1, but it takes 0.044 from ASA 1 vs 2, the one before it. It controls the family-wise error rate just as well as Bonferroni and is never less powerful, so **use Holm rather than Bonferroni**.
- **Benjamini-Hochberg (BH), p = 0.026:** controls something different, the **false discovery rate**: the expected share of false positives among the results you call significant. It's the most lenient of the three. It suits screening many outcomes for leads, not confirming a claim. To get it, each p-value is multiplied by the number of tests and divided by its [rank](../glossary.qmd#rank){.term}, counted from the smallest: here 0.022 × 6 / 5 = 0.026.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔍 Under the hood: Holm and Benjamini-Hochberg by hand

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
by_hand <- adjusted |>
  select(pair, unadjusted) |>
  arrange(unadjusted) |>                                          # the smallest p-value first
  mutate(rank = row_number(),
         times_holm = 6 - rank + 1,                               # Holm: × 6, × 5, ... × 1
         holm = pmin(1, cummax(unadjusted * times_holm)),         # never smaller than the one before it
         times_bh = 6 / rank,                                     # BH: × 6 ÷ rank
         bh = rev(cummin(rev(pmin(1, unadjusted * times_bh)))))   # never larger than the one after it
by_hand |> mutate(across(c(unadjusted, holm, bh), \(p) signif(p, 3)))
```

## Python

```{python}
by_hand = adjusted[["pair", "unadjusted"]].sort_values("unadjusted").reset_index(drop=True)        # the smallest p-value first
by_hand["rank"] = by_hand.index + 1
by_hand["times_holm"] = 6 - by_hand["rank"] + 1                                                    # Holm: × 6, × 5, ... × 1
by_hand["holm"] = (by_hand["unadjusted"] * by_hand["times_holm"]).cummax().clip(upper=1)           # never smaller than the one before it
by_hand["times_bh"] = 6 / by_hand["rank"]                                                          # BH: × 6 ÷ rank
by_hand["bh"] = (by_hand["unadjusted"] * by_hand["times_bh"])[::-1].cummin()[::-1].clip(upper=1)   # never larger than the one after it
print(by_hand.to_string(float_format=lambda p: f"{p:.3g}"))
```
:::

The six p-values are sorted from the smallest to the largest. ASA 1 vs 2 comes fifth: Holm multiplies it by 2 (0.022 × 2 = 0.044), and Benjamini-Hochberg by 6 ÷ 5 = 1.2 (0.022 × 1.2 = 0.026). ASA 3 vs 4 comes last. Holm multiplies it by 1, which leaves 0.030, less than the 0.044 before it, so it takes 0.044. The `holm` and `bh` columns match the ones the software gave above.
:::

```{python}
#| include: false
chk = {"holm_5": float(by_hand["holm"].iloc[4]), "holm_6": float(by_hand["holm"].iloc[5]),
       "bh_2": float(by_hand["bh"].iloc[1]), "bh_5": float(by_hand["bh"].iloc[4])}
```

```{r}
#| include: false
check_agree(list(holm_5 = by_hand$holm[5], holm_6 = by_hand$holm[6], bh_2 = by_hand$bh[2], bh_5 = by_hand$bh[5]),
            reticulate::py$chk)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Watch out: decide the adjustment before you see the p-values
Picking whichever adjustment keeps your favourite result significant is p-hacking. Choose in advance: Holm (or a method built for the test, like Tukey's below) for comparisons you'll report as findings, Benjamini-Hochberg only for exploratory screening. Say in the Methods which you used and how many comparisons it covered.
:::

## After ANOVA: Tukey's HSD and Games-Howell {#after-anova}

After a one-way ANOVA, **Tukey's honestly significant difference** (HSD) compares every pair of group means. It adjusts for all the pairs at once, and gives each difference a CI that's adjusted too. It assumes the groups have similar spreads, like the ANOVA. When they don't (the largest SD is more than about twice the smallest), use **Games-Howell**, the Welch version of Tukey's test.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
cohort |> group_by(asa) |> summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(age), sd = sd(age))   # look first: group sizes, means and SDs

age_anova <- aov(age ~ factor(asa), data = cohort)
summary(age_anova)                                        # the overall test, as on page 8
age_tukey <- TukeyHSD(age_anova)                          # diff, adjusted 95% CI, adjusted p
age_tukey

games_howell <- rstatix::games_howell_test(cohort |> mutate(asa = factor(asa)), age ~ asa)
games_howell |> select(group1, group2, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.adj)
```

## Python

```{python}
print(cohort.groupby("asa")["age"].agg(["count", "mean", "std"]).round(2))   # look first: group sizes, means and SDs
print(pg.anova(data=cohort, dv="age", between="asa"))                        # the overall test, as on page 8

age_tukey = pairwise_tukeyhsd(cohort["age"], cohort["asa"])
print(age_tukey.summary())

games_howell = pg.pairwise_gameshowell(data=cohort, dv="age", between="asa")
print(games_howell[["A", "B", "diff", "se", "pval"]].round(4))
```
:::

```{python}
#| include: false
chk = {"diff_12": float(age_tukey.meandiffs[0]), "low_12": float(age_tukey.confint[0][0]),
       "high_12": float(age_tukey.confint[0][1]), "p_12": float(age_tukey.pvalues[0]), "p_34": float(age_tukey.pvalues[5]),
       "gh_12": float(games_howell["pval"].iloc[0]), "gh_34": float(games_howell["pval"].iloc[5])}
chk_look = {"sd_1": float(cohort.loc[cohort["asa"] == 1, "age"].std()), "sd_4": float(cohort.loc[cohort["asa"] == 4, "age"].std()),
            "f": float(pg.anova(data=cohort, dv="age", between="asa")["F"].iloc[0])}
```

```{r}
#| include: false
tukey <- age_tukey$`factor(asa)`
check_agree(list(diff_12 = tukey["2-1", "diff"], low_12 = tukey["2-1", "lwr"], high_12 = tukey["2-1", "upr"],
                 p_12 = tukey["2-1", "p adj"], p_34 = tukey["4-3", "p adj"],
                 gh_12 = games_howell$p.adj[1], gh_34 = games_howell$p.adj[6]),
            reticulate::py$chk)
check_agree(list(sd_1 = sd(cohort$age[cohort$asa == 1]), sd_4 = sd(cohort$age[cohort$asa == 4]),
                 f = summary(age_anova)[[1]][1, "F value"]), reticulate::py$chk_look)
```

- **The first table:** each ASA class's size, mean age and SD.
- **The ANOVA table:** the overall test from [page 8](../catalog/08-three-plus-unmatched.qmd#one-way-anova), F = 23.9 on 3 and 596 degrees of freedom (`Df` in R; `ddof1` and `ddof2` in Python).
- **diff / meandiff:** the difference in mean age between two ASA classes, in years.
- **lwr, upr / lower, upper:** the 95% CI of that difference, adjusted for all six comparisons.
- **p adj / p-adj:** the adjusted p-value.
- **reject** (Python): True when the adjusted p-value is below 0.05.
- **Games-Howell** shows the same three things under other names: `estimate`, `conf.low`, `conf.high` and `p.adj` in R; `diff` and `pval` in Python, which prints the standard error (`se`) in place of a CI.

Four of the six pairs differ clearly (p < 0.001 or, for ASA 2 vs 4 in the Games-Howell test, p = 0.001). Two don't: ASA 2 patients were 3.6 years older than ASA 1 patients (95% CI −0.4 to 7.7, p = 0.096), and ASA 4 patients 5.3 years older than ASA 3 patients (95% CI −0.3 to 10.9, p = 0.072). Both CIs include 0, and both comparisons involve one of the two small classes (ASA 1 with 36 patients and ASA 4 with 18). The SDs are similar (8.7 to 9.3 years: `sd` in R's first table, `std` in Python's), so Games-Howell reaches the same conclusions.

> **Methods:** Age was compared across ASA classes with one-way ANOVA, followed by Tukey's honestly significant difference test for pairwise comparisons.
>
> **Results:** Across ASA classes, one-way ANOVA gave F(3, 596) = 23.9 (p < 0.001). In pairwise comparisons, the difference in mean age was 5.0 years between ASA 3 and ASA 2 (95% CI 3.0 to 6.9; p < 0.001), 3.6 years between ASA 2 and ASA 1 (95% CI −0.4 to 7.7; p = 0.096) and 5.3 years between ASA 4 and ASA 3 (95% CI −0.3 to 10.9; p = 0.072). Table 2 gives all six pairwise comparisons.

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🔀 R vs Python: Tukey and Games-Howell
R's `TukeyHSD()` and statsmodels' `pairwise_tukeyhsd()` give identical results; R writes the pairs as "2-1" (second group minus first), statsmodels as group1, group2 with meandiff = group2 − group1. For Games-Howell, R needs the rstatix package; in Python, pingouin's `pairwise_gameshowell()` reports `diff` as A − B, so its signs are the reverse of R's estimates. The p-values agree.
:::

## After Kruskal-Wallis: Dunn's test {#after-kruskal-wallis}

**Dunn's test** follows a Kruskal-Wallis test. It compares the groups' mean ranks from the Kruskal-Wallis ranking, so it measures every pair on the same scale. Use it with Holm's adjustment. Running separate Mann-Whitney tests instead re-ranks the data for each pair and needs an adjustment of its own.

Length of stay (LOS) is skewed (most patients go home on day 0 or 1), so it belongs in the rank column. Does it differ across ASA classes?

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
cohort |>
  group_by(asa) |>
  summarise(n = n(), median = median(los_days),
            q1 = quantile(los_days, 0.25), q3 = quantile(los_days, 0.75))

los_kw <- kruskal.test(los_days ~ factor(asa), data = cohort)
los_kw
dunn <- rstatix::dunn_test(cohort, los_days ~ asa, p.adjust.method = "holm")
dunn |> select(group1, group2, statistic, p, p.adj)
```

## Python

```{python}
print(cohort.groupby("asa")["los_days"].describe()[["count", "25%", "50%", "75%"]])

los_kw = stats.kruskal(*[group["los_days"] for _, group in cohort.groupby("asa")])
print(los_kw.statistic, los_kw.pvalue)
dunn = sp.posthoc_dunn(cohort, val_col="los_days", group_col="asa", p_adjust="holm")
print(dunn.round(4))                                           # adjusted p-values
```
:::

```{python}
#| include: false
chk = {"h": float(los_kw.statistic), "p_12": float(dunn.loc[1, 2]), "p_23": float(dunn.loc[2, 3]),
       "p_24": float(dunn.loc[2, 4]), "p_34": float(dunn.loc[3, 4])}
```

```{r}
#| include: false
check_agree(list(h = unname(los_kw$statistic), p_12 = dunn$p.adj[1], p_23 = dunn$p.adj[4],
                 p_24 = dunn$p.adj[5], p_34 = dunn$p.adj[6]),
            reticulate::py$chk)
```

- **Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = 24.286** (R; the first number Python prints): the H statistic, 24.3. **df = 3:** four classes minus one (Python doesn't print it). **p < 0.001:** R prints `2.177e-05` and Python the same number with more digits, which is [scientific notation](../glossary.qmd#scientific-notation){.term} for 0.00002177. LOS differs somewhere across the classes.
- **Dunn's test:** ASA 1 differs from every other class (adjusted p = 0.011 against ASA 2, p < 0.001 against ASAs 3 and 4), and ASA 2 differs from ASAs 3 (p = 0.047) and 4 (p = 0.022). There was no clear evidence of a difference between ASA 3 and 4 (p = 0.061).
- **The statistic** in R's output is a z score: positive means the second group's ranks are higher (longer stays).

> **Results:** The median length of stay was 0 days (IQR 0 to 0) in ASA 1 and 1 day (IQR 0.25 to 3.5) in ASA 4 (Kruskal-Wallis H = 24.3, df = 3, p < 0.001). In Dunn's tests with Holm's adjustment, p ≤ 0.011 for ASA 1 against each other class and p = 0.061 for ASA 3 against ASA 4.

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🔀 R vs Python: Dunn's test
Both correct the z scores for tied ranks, which matter here because many patients share a LOS of 0 or 1 day, and both give the same adjusted p-values. R's rstatix returns one row per pair; scikit-posthocs' `posthoc_dunn()` returns a square table of p-values with the groups on both sides.
:::

## After chi-square: pairwise Fisher's exact tests {#after-chi-square}

After a chi-square (or Fisher) test on a table with three or more groups, compare the groups two at a time with **Fisher's exact test**, then adjust with Holm. Take 90-day complications across the four ASA classes. Two of the [expected counts](../glossary.qmd#expected-count){.term} are below 5 (3.06 in ASA 1 and 1.53 in ASA 4, in the second table below), too few for the chi-square test ([page 8](../catalog/08-three-plus-unmatched.qmd#chi-square)), so the overall test is Fisher's exact test too:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
#| warning: false
complications <- table(asa = cohort$asa, complication = cohort$complication_90d)
complications
chisq.test(complications)$expected                # two expected counts are below 5
fisher_overall <- fisher.test(complications)      # overall: expected counts are too small for chi-square
fisher_overall

pairwise_fisher <- rstatix::pairwise_fisher_test(complications, p.adjust.method = "holm")
pairwise_fisher
```

## Python

```{python}
complications = pd.crosstab(cohort["asa"], cohort["complication_90d"])
print(complications)
print(stats.chi2_contingency(complications).expected_freq.round(2))   # two expected counts are below 5

fisher_p = []
for a, b in asa_pairs:
    two_classes = complications.loc[[a, b]]                     # a 2 x 2 table for this pair
    fisher_p.append(stats.fisher_exact(two_classes).pvalue)
fisher_holm = multipletests(fisher_p, method="holm")[1]
print(pd.DataFrame({"pair": [f"{a} vs {b}" for a, b in asa_pairs], "p": fisher_p, "p_holm": fisher_holm}).round(4))
```
:::

```{python}
#| include: false
chk = {"p_14": float(fisher_p[2]), "holm_14": float(fisher_holm[2]), "holm_24": float(fisher_holm[4]),
       "holm_12": float(fisher_holm[0])}
chk_expected = {"smallest": float(stats.chi2_contingency(complications).expected_freq.min()),
                "asa_1": float(stats.chi2_contingency(complications).expected_freq[0, 1])}
```

```{r}
#| include: false
check_agree(list(p_14 = pairwise_fisher$p[3], holm_14 = pairwise_fisher$p.adj[3], holm_24 = pairwise_fisher$p.adj[5],
                 holm_12 = pairwise_fisher$p.adj[1]),
            reticulate::py$chk)
check_agree(list(smallest = min(suppressWarnings(chisq.test(complications))$expected),
                 asa_1 = suppressWarnings(chisq.test(complications))$expected["1", "1"]), reticulate::py$chk_expected)
```

The overall Fisher test says the complication rate differs across ASA classes (p = 0.016; R prints 0.01587). scipy can only estimate this p-value for a table larger than 2 × 2 ([page 8](../catalog/08-three-plus-unmatched.qmd#chi-square)), so the Python tab runs the pairs only. But no single pair differs clearly after Holm's adjustment: the closest is ASA 1 vs ASA 4 (0 of 36 vs 4 of 18 patients; p = 0.010 unadjusted, 0.058 adjusted). [A later section](#overall-test-first) explains why that can happen.

## After repeated-measures ANOVA: paired t tests {#after-repeated-measures-anova}

[Page 9](../catalog/09-three-plus-matched.qmd#repeated-measures-anova) found that PROMIS physical function changed over the first year, in 328 procedures measured at all four visits. To say *when* it changed, compare every pair of visits with a **paired t test** and adjust with Holm:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
pf <- proms |>
  select(case_id, visit, promis_pf) |>
  group_by(case_id) |>
  filter(all(!is.na(promis_pf))) |>                  # patients measured at all four visits
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(visit = factor(visit, levels = c("preop", "6wk", "3mo", "1yr"))) |>
  arrange(case_id, visit)                           # paired tests match rows by position

pf |> group_by(visit) |> summarise(mean = mean(promis_pf))   # mean score at each visit

pf_pairs <- rstatix::pairwise_t_test(pf, promis_pf ~ visit, paired = TRUE, p.adjust.method = "holm")
pf_pairs |> select(group1, group2, n1, statistic, df, p.adj)
```

## Python

```{python}
pf = proms[["case_id", "visit", "promis_pf"]]
pf = pf[pf.groupby("case_id")["promis_pf"].transform(lambda scores: scores.notna().all())]

print(pf.groupby("visit")["promis_pf"].mean().round(1)[["preop", "6wk", "3mo", "1yr"]])   # mean score at each visit

pf_pairs = pg.pairwise_tests(data=pf, dv="promis_pf", within="visit", subject="case_id", padjust="holm")
print(pf_pairs[["A", "B", "T", "dof", "p_corr"]])
```
:::

```{python}
#| include: false
def paired_t(a, b):
    row = pf_pairs[((pf_pairs["A"] == a) & (pf_pairs["B"] == b)) | ((pf_pairs["A"] == b) & (pf_pairs["B"] == a))]
    return float(abs(row["T"].iloc[0]))
chk = {"t_pre_6wk": paired_t("preop", "6wk"), "t_3mo_1yr": paired_t("3mo", "1yr"), "t_pre_1yr": paired_t("preop", "1yr")}
chk_means = {"preop": float(pf.loc[pf["visit"] == "preop", "promis_pf"].mean()),
             "one_year": float(pf.loc[pf["visit"] == "1yr", "promis_pf"].mean())}
```

```{r}
#| include: false
check_agree(list(t_pre_6wk = abs(pf_pairs$statistic[1]), t_3mo_1yr = abs(pf_pairs$statistic[6]),
                 t_pre_1yr = abs(pf_pairs$statistic[3])),
            reticulate::py$chk)
check_agree(list(preop = mean(pf$promis_pf[pf$visit == "preop"]), one_year = mean(pf$promis_pf[pf$visit == "1yr"])),
            reticulate::py$chk_means)
```

The mean T-score was 36.1 before surgery, 39.4 at 6 weeks, 44.9 at 3 months and 48.2 at 1 year (the first output). Every pair of visits differs: all adjusted p-values are below 0.001, and the largest is printed as `5.59e-13` in R. R's `statistic` is negative because it subtracts the later visit from the earlier one: pre-op minus 6 weeks gives t = −7.98. Python subtracts the other way round and prints 7.98. With 328 procedures and changes this large, the adjustment changes nothing. It matters most when results sit near p = 0.05.

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🔀 R vs Python: which way round
pingouin sorts the visits alphabetically and subtracts the second from the first, so its t statistics are negative where R's are positive, or the other way round. Compare their sizes. rstatix needs the rows in the same patient order within every visit, so sort by patient first.
:::

## After Friedman: pairwise Wilcoxon or Conover tests {#after-friedman}

After a Friedman test, compare pairs of visits with **Wilcoxon signed-rank tests** and Holm's adjustment, or with **Conover's test**, which reuses the Friedman ranks (as Dunn's test does after Kruskal-Wallis) and is often more powerful. [Page 9](../catalog/09-three-plus-matched.qmd#friedman) found that the EFAS score changed between 6 weeks, 3 months and 12 months in 50 patients with a boot:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
efas_boot <- trial |>
  filter(arm == "boot", visit %in% c("6wk", "3mo", "12mo")) |>
  select(patient_id, visit, efas) |>
  group_by(patient_id) |>
  filter(all(!is.na(efas))) |>                         # patients scored at all three visits
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(visit = factor(visit, levels = c("6wk", "3mo", "12mo"))) |>
  arrange(patient_id, visit)

efas_boot |> group_by(visit) |> summarise(n = n(), median = median(efas))   # patients and median score at each visit

efas_pairs <- rstatix::pairwise_wilcox_test(efas_boot, efas ~ visit, paired = TRUE, exact = FALSE, correct = FALSE,
                                            p.adjust.method = "holm")
efas_pairs |> select(group1, group2, statistic, p, p.adj)

efas_conover <- PMCMRplus::frdAllPairsConoverTest(y = efas_boot$efas, groups = efas_boot$visit, blocks = efas_boot$patient_id,
                                                  p.adjust.method = "holm")
signif(efas_conover$p.value, 3)          # printing efas_conover itself shows these only as "<2e-16"
```

## Python

```{python}
visits = ["6wk", "3mo", "12mo"]
efas_boot = trial[(trial["arm"] == "boot") & trial["visit"].isin(visits)]
efas_wide = efas_boot.pivot(index="patient_id", columns="visit", values="efas")[visits].dropna()
print(len(efas_wide))                                    # patients scored at all three visits
print(efas_wide.median())                                # median score at each visit

wilcoxon = {}
for a, b in [("6wk", "3mo"), ("6wk", "12mo"), ("3mo", "12mo")]:
    wilcoxon[(a, b)] = stats.wilcoxon(efas_wide[a], efas_wide[b], method="approx", correction=False)
    print(a, b, wilcoxon[(a, b)].statistic)
print(multipletests([test.pvalue for test in wilcoxon.values()], method="holm")[1])

efas_conover = sp.posthoc_conover_friedman(efas_wide, p_adjust="holm")
print(efas_conover)
```
:::

```{python}
#| include: false
chk = {"v_6wk_3mo": float(wilcoxon[("6wk", "3mo")].statistic), "v_3mo_12mo": float(wilcoxon[("3mo", "12mo")].statistic),
       "n": float(len(efas_wide)),
       # p-values this small would pass any check on their own, so compare their logarithms
       "log10_p_6wk_12mo": float(np.log10(efas_conover.loc["6wk", "12mo"])),
       "log10_p_3mo_12mo": float(np.log10(efas_conover.loc["3mo", "12mo"]))}
chk_medians = {"first": float(efas_wide["6wk"].median()), "last": float(efas_wide["12mo"].median())}
```

```{r}
#| include: false
check_agree(list(v_6wk_3mo = efas_pairs$statistic[1], v_3mo_12mo = efas_pairs$statistic[3],
                 n = n_distinct(efas_boot$patient_id),
                 log10_p_6wk_12mo = log10(efas_conover$p.value["12mo", "6wk"]),
                 log10_p_3mo_12mo = log10(efas_conover$p.value["12mo", "3mo"])),
            reticulate::py$chk)
check_agree(list(first = median(efas_boot$efas[efas_boot$visit == "6wk"]), last = median(efas_boot$efas[efas_boot$visit == "12mo"])),
            reticulate::py$chk_medians)
```

The median EFAS score was 12.5 at 6 weeks, 17 at 3 months and 20 at 12 months, in 50 patients (the first lines of the output). All three pairs differ (adjusted p < 0.001 with either method).

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🔀 R vs Python: the statistic
R's `wilcox.test()` reports V, the sum of the positive ranks; scipy reports the smaller of the two rank sums. Here both are the same number, because the later visit scores higher for most patients. Conover's test needs the PMCMRplus package in R and scikit-posthocs in Python; they give the same p-values. Printing PMCMRplus's result shows any p-value below 2 × 10⁻¹⁶ only as "<2e-16", so print its `$p.value` table to see them.
:::

## After Cochran's Q: pairwise McNemar tests {#after-cochran-q}

After Cochran's Q, compare pairs of visits with **McNemar's test** and adjust with Holm. [Page 9](../catalog/09-three-plus-matched.qmd#cochran-q) found that walking-aid use changed over the year in 328 procedures assessed at all four visits:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
aid <- proms |>
  select(case_id, visit, walking_aid) |>
  group_by(case_id) |>
  filter(all(!is.na(walking_aid))) |>               # patients assessed at all four visits
  ungroup() |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = visit, values_from = walking_aid)

nrow(aid)                                                            # procedures assessed at all four visits
round(100 * colMeans(aid[, c("preop", "6wk", "3mo", "1yr")]), 1)     # % using a walking aid at each visit

visit_pairs <- combn(c("preop", "6wk", "3mo", "1yr"), 2)    # six pairs, one per column
mcnemar_p <- apply(visit_pairs, 2, function(pair) {
  mcnemar.test(table(factor(aid[[pair[1]]], levels = 0:1), factor(aid[[pair[2]]], levels = 0:1)))$p.value
})
mcnemar_results <- tibble(first = visit_pairs[1, ], second = visit_pairs[2, ],
                          p = mcnemar_p, p_holm = p.adjust(mcnemar_p, method = "holm"))
mcnemar_results
```

## Python

```{python}
aid = proms.pivot(index="case_id", columns="visit", values="walking_aid").dropna()   # assessed at all four visits
print(len(aid))                                                           # procedures assessed at all four visits
print((100 * aid[["preop", "6wk", "3mo", "1yr"]].mean()).round(1))        # % using a walking aid at each visit

mcnemar_p = []
visit_pairs = list(itertools.combinations(["preop", "6wk", "3mo", "1yr"], 2))
for first, second in visit_pairs:
    pair_table = pd.crosstab(aid[first], aid[second]).reindex(index=[0, 1], columns=[0, 1], fill_value=0)
    mcnemar_p.append(mcnemar(pair_table, exact=False, correction=True).pvalue)   # as R's mcnemar.test()
mcnemar_holm = multipletests(mcnemar_p, method="holm")[1]
print(pd.DataFrame({"pair": visit_pairs, "p": mcnemar_p, "p_holm": mcnemar_holm}))
```
:::

```{python}
#| include: false
chk = {"p_pre_3mo": float(mcnemar_p[1]), "holm_pre_3mo": float(mcnemar_holm[1]), "n": float(len(aid))}
chk_aid = {"preop": float(aid["preop"].mean()), "six_weeks": float(aid["6wk"].mean()), "one_year": float(aid["1yr"].mean())}
```

```{r}
#| include: false
check_agree(list(p_pre_3mo = mcnemar_results$p[2], holm_pre_3mo = mcnemar_results$p_holm[2], n = nrow(aid)),
            reticulate::py$chk)
check_agree(list(preop = mean(aid$preop), six_weeks = mean(aid$`6wk`), one_year = mean(aid$`1yr`)), reticulate::py$chk_aid)
```

A walking aid was used in 34.8% of the 328 procedures before surgery, 59.1% at 6 weeks, 24.4% at 3 months and 10.4% at 1 year (the first two outputs). Every pair of visits differs after adjustment (the `p_holm` column). The largest adjusted p-value is for pre-op against 3 months: 0.005, printed in scientific notation as `4.66e- 3` in R and `4.658779e-03` in Python.

## After a log-rank test: pairwise survival comparisons {#after-log-rank}

[Page 13](../survival/13-kaplan-meier.qmd#log-rank) found that revision-free survival differs across implants A, B and C. To say which implants differ, run the **log-rank test for each pair** and adjust with Holm. A Cox model gives the matching effect sizes: refit it with a different reference group to get the hazard ratio for any pair.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
survdiff(Surv(followup_years, revised) ~ implant, data = cohort)   # the overall log-rank test, as on page 13

implant_pairs <- combn(c("A", "B", "C"), 2)
logrank <- apply(implant_pairs, 2, function(pair) {
  two_implants <- cohort |> filter(implant %in% pair)
  test <- survdiff(Surv(followup_years, revised) ~ implant, data = two_implants)
  c(chisq = test$chisq, p = test$pvalue)
})
logrank_results <- tibble(first = implant_pairs[1, ], second = implant_pairs[2, ], chisq = logrank["chisq", ],
                          p = logrank["p", ], p_holm = p.adjust(logrank["p", ], method = "holm"))
logrank_results

# hazard ratios against implant B instead of A
cohort <- cohort |> mutate(implant_vs_b = relevel(factor(implant), ref = "B"))
implant_vs_b_model <- coxph(Surv(followup_years, revised) ~ implant_vs_b, data = cohort)
summary(implant_vs_b_model)$conf.int
```

## Python

```{python}
overall_logrank = multivariate_logrank_test(cohort["followup_years"], cohort["implant"], cohort["revised"])
print(overall_logrank.test_statistic, overall_logrank.p_value)   # the overall log-rank test, as on page 13

pairwise_logrank = pairwise_logrank_test(cohort["followup_years"], cohort["implant"], cohort["revised"])
logrank_p = pairwise_logrank.summary["p"]
logrank_holm = multipletests(logrank_p, method="holm")[1]
print(pd.DataFrame({"chisq": pairwise_logrank.summary["test_statistic"], "p": logrank_p, "p_holm": logrank_holm}))

# hazard ratios against implant B instead of A: the first category is the reference
cohort["implant_vs_b"] = pd.Categorical(cohort["implant"], categories=["B", "A", "C"])
implant_vs_b = CoxPHFitter().fit(cohort[["followup_years", "revised", "implant_vs_b"]],
                                 duration_col="followup_years", event_col="revised", formula="implant_vs_b",
                                 fit_options={"precision": 1e-12})
print(implant_vs_b.summary[["exp(coef)", "exp(coef) lower 95%", "exp(coef) upper 95%"]])
```
:::

```{python}
#| include: false
hr_rows = implant_vs_b.summary
chk = {"p_ab": float(logrank_p.iloc[0]), "holm_ab": float(logrank_holm[0]), "chisq_bc": float(pairwise_logrank.summary["test_statistic"].iloc[2]),
       "hr_cb": float(hr_rows.loc["implant_vs_b[T.C]", "exp(coef)"]),
       "low_cb": float(hr_rows.loc["implant_vs_b[T.C]", "exp(coef) lower 95%"]),
       "high_cb": float(hr_rows.loc["implant_vs_b[T.C]", "exp(coef) upper 95%"])}
chk_overall = {"chisq": float(overall_logrank.test_statistic), "hr_ab": float(hr_rows.loc["implant_vs_b[T.A]", "exp(coef)"])}
```

```{r}
#| include: false
implant_vs_b_hr <- summary(implant_vs_b_model)$conf.int
check_agree(list(p_ab = logrank_results$p[1], holm_ab = logrank_results$p_holm[1], chisq_bc = logrank_results$chisq[3],
                 hr_cb = implant_vs_b_hr["implant_vs_bC", "exp(coef)"], low_cb = implant_vs_b_hr["implant_vs_bC", "lower .95"],
                 high_cb = implant_vs_b_hr["implant_vs_bC", "upper .95"]),
            reticulate::py$chk)
check_agree(list(chisq = survdiff(Surv(followup_years, revised) ~ implant, data = cohort)$chisq,
                 hr_ab = implant_vs_b_hr["implant_vs_bA", "exp(coef)"]), reticulate::py$chk_overall)
```

Implant C differs from both A and B (adjusted p < 0.001 for each). There was no clear evidence of a difference between A and B (p = 0.520; hazard ratio for A against B 1.22, 95% CI 0.67 to 2.24, the first row of the Cox output). Against implant B, implant C's hazard ratio was 3.75 (95% CI 2.14 to 6.58, the second row); against implant A it was 3.07 (95% CI 1.85 to 5.09; [page 8](../catalog/08-three-plus-unmatched.qmd#cox)). R's `exp(-coef)` column is the same ratio the other way round. The first output is the overall test: χ² = 33.5 on 2 degrees of freedom (Python prints the statistic and the p-value only).

> **Results:** The log-rank test for revision-free survival across implants gave χ² = 33.5 (df = 2, p < 0.001). In pairwise log-rank tests with Holm's adjustment, p < 0.001 for implant C against implant A and against implant B, and p = 0.520 for implant A against implant B.

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🔀 R vs Python: pairwise log-rank tests
lifelines has `pairwise_logrank_test()`, which runs every pair at once and leaves the adjustment to you. lifelines' Cox model stops iterating slightly early by default, so, as on [page 14](../survival/14-cox-regression.qmd), the Python Cox fit passes `fit_options={"precision": 1e-12}` to match R's hazard ratios. R's survival package has no pairwise function, so the R code loops over the pairs; the survminer package's `pairwise_survdiff()` does the same in one call. To change the reference group, R uses `relevel()`; lifelines uses the first category of a pandas `Categorical`.
:::

## Do you need a significant overall test first? {#overall-test-first}

A common rule says: only run post-hoc tests if the overall test (the ANOVA, Kruskal-Wallis or chi-square) is significant. It comes from **Fisher's least significant difference** method, which runs unadjusted pairwise tests and relies on the overall test as a gate. That gate only fully protects you with three groups.

The tests on this page don't need the gate. Tukey's HSD and Games-Howell control the family-wise error rate on their own, and so do Dunn's test and any other set of pairwise tests once Holm's adjustment is applied. Requiring a significant overall test first just makes them stricter than they need to be.

The two kinds of test can also disagree, and that's not a contradiction:
- **A significant overall test with no significant pair**, as with complications by ASA class above (overall p = 0.016; no pair below 0.05 after adjustment). The overall test pools the evidence from all four classes, while each pair uses only two of them, and the ASA 1 and ASA 4 groups are small. Report it as it is: complication rates differed across ASA classes overall, but no single pair of classes differed clearly.
- **A significant pair with no significant overall test.** This can happen when one pair differs and the others don't, diluting the overall test.

What to do:
1. **Decide before you look at the data** which comparisons you'll make: every pair, or a few planned ones.
2. **If your question is about pairs, go straight to an adjusted pairwise method.** The overall test is optional; report it if your readers expect it.
3. **Never run unadjusted pairwise tests you didn't plan**, whatever the overall test says.
4. **Say what you did** in the Methods.

## Planned comparisons and how to report them {#planned-comparisons}

Not every comparison is a fishing trip. A study comparing a new implant with the standard one has one **pre-specified** comparison, named in the protocol before any data were collected. It needs no adjustment, because it isn't one of many. If you planned three comparisons, adjust for three, not for every possible pair.

Everything else is **exploratory**: comparisons chosen after seeing the data, or a scan across many outcomes. Adjust for every comparison you looked at, not only the ones you report, and label the results exploratory: they suggest questions for the next study, not conclusions.

> **Methods:** Pairwise comparisons after the omnibus tests used Tukey's honestly significant difference test (after ANOVA), Dunn's test (after Kruskal-Wallis) and Fisher's exact tests (after chi-square), with Holm's adjustment for multiple comparisons where the method did not adjust itself. All pairwise comparisons were exploratory.
>
> **Results:** Across ASA classes, one-way ANOVA gave F(3, 596) = 23.9 (p < 0.001); in pairwise comparisons, the difference in mean age between ASA 3 and ASA 2 was 5.0 years (95% CI 3.0 to 6.9; p < 0.001). Table 2 gives all six pairwise comparisons.

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Watch out: report every comparison you ran
Running ten comparisons and reporting the two significant ones hides how many chances you had. Give the number of comparisons and the adjustment in the Methods, and put the full set of pairwise results in a table or supplement.
:::

```{r}

  round(pf_pairs$statistic[1], 2) == -7.98, format(signif(max(pf_pairs$p.adj), 3)) == "5.59e-13",
  tapply(efas_boot$efas, efas_boot$visit, median) == c(12.5, 17, 20),
  round(100 * colMeans(aid[, c("preop", "6wk", "3mo", "1yr")]), 1) == c(34.8, 59.1, 24.4, 10.4),
  which.max(mcnemar_results$p_holm) == 2, format(signif(mcnemar_results$p_holm[2], 3)) == "0.00466",
  round(implant_vs_b_hr["implant_vs_bA", c("exp(coef)", "lower .95", "upper .95")], 2) == c(1.22, 0.67, 2.24),
  # exercise solutions (recomputed here: the guard runs before the solution chunks)
  all(tukey_bmi[, "p adj"] < 0.01), round(tukey_bmi["2-1", c("diff", "lwr", "upr")], 1) == c(2.9, 0.6, 5.2),
  round(tukey_bmi["4-3", c("diff", "lwr", "upr")], 1) == c(4.1, 0.9, 7.2),
  round(tukey_bmi["2-1", "p adj"], 3) == 0.007, round(tukey_bmi["4-3", "p adj"], 3) == 0.006,
  names(which(p.adjust(sex_p, "holm") < 0.05)) == "sleep_apnea", round(sex_p[["hypertension"]], 3) == 0.135,
  all(p.adjust(sex_p, "BH")[names(sex_p) != "sleep_apnea"] > 0.4),
  nrow(aid3) == 345, all(p.adjust(aid3_p, "holm") < 0.001),
  round(100 * colMeans(aid3[, c("6wk", "3mo", "1yr")]), 1) == c(58.8, 25.2, 10.7),
  colSums(aid3[, c("6wk", "3mo", "1yr")]) == c(203, 87, 37)
)
```

## Exercises {#exercises}

The solutions use the packages and data loaded in the sections above, so run the page from the top first.

**1.** [Page 8's exercise 1](../catalog/08-three-plus-unmatched.qmd#exercises) found that BMI differs across ASA classes. Which pairs of classes differ? Use Tukey's HSD.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
TukeyHSD(aov(bmi ~ factor(asa), data = cohort))
```

## Python

```{python}
print(pairwise_tukeyhsd(cohort["bmi"], cohort["asa"]).summary())
```
:::

> **Results:** In Tukey's HSD, all six pairwise differences in mean BMI had adjusted p < 0.01, including ASA 2 vs 1 (2.9 kg/m², 95% CI 0.6 to 5.2; p = 0.007) and ASA 4 vs 3 (4.1 kg/m², 95% CI 0.9 to 7.2; p = 0.006).

Every pair differs, and mean BMI rises with each step in ASA class. The least certain differences involve the two small classes, ASA 1 and ASA 4.
:::

**2.** A colleague compares men and women on six yes/no characteristics (diabetes, hypertension, sleep apnea, readmission, complications and discharge to a rehabilitation clinic) with Fisher's exact test. Which adjustment fits, and which differences survive it?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
This is a screen across several outcomes with no single planned comparison, so the results are exploratory. Holm's adjustment keeps the chance of any false positive at 5%; Benjamini-Hochberg is acceptable for a screen, as long as the results are labeled exploratory.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
yes_no <- cohort |> mutate(rehab = as.integer(discharge == "rehabilitation clinic"))
characteristics <- c("diabetes", "hypertension", "sleep_apnea", "readmit_90d", "complication_90d", "rehab")
by_sex_p <- sapply(characteristics, function(v) fisher.test(table(yes_no$sex, yes_no[[v]]))$p.value)
round(cbind(unadjusted = by_sex_p, holm = p.adjust(by_sex_p, "holm"), bh = p.adjust(by_sex_p, "BH")), 4)
```

## Python

```{python}
cohort["rehab"] = (cohort["discharge"] == "rehabilitation clinic").astype(int)
characteristics = ["diabetes", "hypertension", "sleep_apnea", "readmit_90d", "complication_90d", "rehab"]
by_sex_p = [stats.fisher_exact(pd.crosstab(cohort["sex"], cohort[v])).pvalue for v in characteristics]
print(pd.DataFrame({"unadjusted": by_sex_p, "holm": multipletests(by_sex_p, method="holm")[1],
                    "bh": multipletests(by_sex_p, method="fdr_bh")[1]}, index=characteristics).round(4))
```
:::

Only sleep apnea differs between men and women after either adjustment (adjusted p < 0.001). Hypertension's unadjusted p = 0.135 was never close, and every other characteristic's Benjamini-Hochberg p-value is above 0.4.
:::

**3.** Leaving out the pre-op visit, which pairs of visits differ in walking-aid use (6 weeks, 3 months, 1 year)? Write the Results sentence.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
later <- proms |>
  filter(visit != "preop") |>
  select(case_id, visit, walking_aid) |>
  group_by(case_id) |>
  filter(all(!is.na(walking_aid))) |>
  ungroup() |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = visit, values_from = walking_aid)
nrow(later)
colSums(later[, c("6wk", "3mo", "1yr")])                     # walking-aid users at each visit
round(100 * colMeans(later[, c("6wk", "3mo", "1yr")]), 1)    # the same, as percentages

later_pairs <- combn(c("6wk", "3mo", "1yr"), 2)
later_p <- apply(later_pairs, 2, function(pair) {
  mcnemar.test(table(factor(later[[pair[1]]], levels = 0:1), factor(later[[pair[2]]], levels = 0:1)))$p.value
})
p.adjust(later_p, method = "holm")
```

## Python

```{python}
later = proms[proms["visit"] != "preop"].pivot(index="case_id", columns="visit", values="walking_aid").dropna()
print(len(later), later[["6wk", "3mo", "1yr"]].sum().astype(int).to_list())    # walking-aid users at each visit
print((100 * later[["6wk", "3mo", "1yr"]].mean()).round(1).to_list())             # the same, as percentages

later_p = []
for first, second in itertools.combinations(["6wk", "3mo", "1yr"], 2):
    pair_table = pd.crosstab(later[first], later[second]).reindex(index=[0, 1], columns=[0, 1], fill_value=0)
    later_p.append(mcnemar(pair_table, exact=False, correction=True).pvalue)
print(multipletests(later_p, method="holm")[1])
```
:::

> **Results:** Among 345 procedures assessed at all three visits, a walking aid was used in 203 (58.8%) at 6 weeks, 87 (25.2%) at 3 months and 37 (10.7%) at 1 year; in McNemar tests with Holm's adjustment, p < 0.001 for every pair of visits.
:::
